strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in video-language models: scaling long-video understanding without discarding large amounts of visual evidence through irreversible token compression.

VideoNSA is a plausible and practically motivated adaptation of Native Sparse Attention to multimodal video inputs, with a sensible hybrid design that keeps dense/GQA-style behavior for text while applying sparse attention over video tokens.

The experimental coverage is broad: the paper evaluates long-form video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial/spatial-memory benchmarks, and compares against dense Qwen2.5-VL, quantization, token-compression methods, and several training-free sparse attention baselines.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses beyond headline accuracy, including branch combinations, context allocation, attention budget allocation, gate behavior, branch latency, and attention-sink analysis.
Training and evaluation settings are described with enough high-level detail to understand the implementation choices, and the 128K-context scaling experiments are relevant to the claimed use case.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than strong. The central mechanism is largely an adaptation of existing Native Sparse Attention, and the paper does not clearly establish which aspects are technically new beyond applying NSA selectively to video tokens in Qwen2.5-VL.

The empirical gains are mixed and often modest. VideoNSA improves over dense Qwen2.5-VL on several benchmarks, but the margins are small on LongVideoBench and MLVU, ties MInference on LongTimeScope, and is below XAttention/MInference on VSIBench in the main table. This weakens claims of consistent superiority.

The efficiency evaluation is incomplete for a paper whose main motivation is scalable attention. The paper reports branch latency, but does not provide a clear end-to-end speed, memory, throughput, or quality-efficiency Pareto comparison against dense FlashAttention and sparse/token-compression baselines under matched hardware and sequence lengths.

The baseline comparison is potentially unfair or under-controlled. Most competing efficient methods are training-free while VideoNSA receives expensive end-to-end training requiring 4600 H100 GPU hours; the dense SFT baseline appears to underperform due to data quality, making it unclear whether gains come from sparse architecture, training recipe, or other implementation details.

The branch ablation is difficult to interpret. Single-branch and two-branch variants collapse substantially, but the paper does not make clear whether these variants are retrained or only disabled at inference, so the results may reflect distribution shift rather than intrinsic branch necessity.

Statistical reliability is not addressed. There are no confidence intervals, repeated runs, seed variation, or significance tests, despite small benchmark differences and known variability in multimodal evaluation.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, including statements about near-linear scalability, reliable extrapolation, and broad advancement of video understanding. The paper demonstrates promising scaling behavior in selected settings, but not enough to support these general claims.

Reproducibility is still limited: the project/code/model fields are blank in the manuscript, and important details such as exact sparse kernels, hardware setup for latency, prompt templates, seed handling, and full baseline tuning procedures are not sufficiently specified.

The paper has presentation issues, including grammar errors, inconsistent terminology and table formatting, duplicated or confusing appendix references, and occasional formula/notation ambiguity. These do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence in the polish and precision expected at a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely bottleneck in video-language models: extending video context without dense quadratic attention over very long visual token sequences.

The proposed hybrid design is plausible: applying learnable sparse attention to video tokens while preserving dense/GQA-style attention for text is a reasonable engineering choice for maintaining instruction-following behavior.
The empirical section covers several relevant benchmark families, including long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial/spatial-temporal tasks.

The paper includes useful diagnostic analyses of branch combinations, context allocation, attention budget allocation, gating behavior, and branch-level latency, which are more extensive than a minimal benchmark-only submission.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The core mechanism is largely an adaptation of Native Sparse Attention to video tokens in Qwen2.5-VL, and the paper does not make a convincing case that the algorithmic contribution is substantially new beyond this application and engineering integration.

The headline empirical gains are small and inconsistent. VideoNSA improves over Qwen2.5-VL by only about 1.3 on LongVideoBench, 0.6 on MLVU, 2.7 on TimeScope, and 3.9 on Tomato, ties MInference on LongTimeScope, and is below MInference/Tri-Shape on VSIBench. This does not support claims of consistently or significantly outperforming existing methods.

The comparison is not fully convincing because VideoNSA receives expensive end-to-end training while most sparse/compression baselines are training-free. The dense SFT baseline performs worse than the base model, which the authors attribute to limited data quality, making it hard to isolate whether gains come from NSA, training recipe, data selection, or hyperparameter choices.

Efficiency claims are under-supported. The paper emphasizes hardware-aware and near-linear efficiency, but reports only limited branch-level latency analysis rather than complete end-to-end prefill/decode latency, throughput, memory, and quality-efficiency tradeoffs against dense FlashAttention and sparse baselines under identical hardware settings.

The ablations do not cleanly establish the necessity of each design choice. Single-branch and two-branch variants collapse heavily, but it is unclear whether these variants are trained comparably, whether gate/branch removal creates distribution shift, or whether simpler sparse/local baselines with matched training would close the gap.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, scaling to 128K is claimed as reliable, but some benchmark optima appear around 64K and performance is task-dependent; the 3.6% attention-budget claim is not paired with a complete wall-clock/memory comparison showing practical superiority.

Reproducibility is weak for a top-tier submission. The abstract lists project page, code, and model fields but leaves them blank, and the method requires 4600 H100 GPU hours, making independent reproduction difficult without released code, checkpoints, kernels, and exact data filtering scripts.

The paper has many presentation and quality-control issues, including typos, duplicated or inconsistent table references, awkward wording, and minor numerical inconsistencies between main and appendix tables. These issues reduce confidence in the care of the experimental reporting.
The ethics statement is generic and unsupported; it asserts safeguards and bias mitigation without describing concrete procedures or measurements.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely bottleneck in video-language models: scaling long-video understanding without discarding visual tokens through irreversible compression.
The proposed VideoNSA system is practically motivated, combining dense attention for text with learnable sparse attention for video tokens in a hardware-aware way.

Evaluation is broad, covering long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial/spatial-reasoning benchmarks, with comparisons to dense Qwen2.5-VL, token-compression methods, and sparse-attention baselines.

The paper includes useful ablations and analyses beyond headline accuracy, including branch ablations, context scaling to 128K tokens, attention-budget allocation, gate behavior, latency by branch, and attention-sink analysis.

Results are generally positive: VideoNSA is competitive or best on several benchmarks, with particularly clear gains on Tomato, TimeScope, LongTimeScope, and VSIBench relative to the dense base model.
weaknesses: The core novelty is somewhat incremental: the main contribution is adapting existing Native Sparse Attention to video tokens in Qwen2.5-VL, and the paper could more clearly distinguish what is conceptually new beyond this adaptation and engineering integration.

Accuracy gains over strong sparse-attention baselines are often modest or inconsistent. For example, VideoNSA ties MInference on LongTimeScope, is below MInference/XAttention on VSIBench in some tables, and improves LongVideoBench/MLVU only slightly over the dense baseline.

The comparison is not fully controlled: VideoNSA is trained end-to-end, while many competing sparse/token-compression baselines are training-free. A stronger study would include similarly fine-tuned sparse baselines or explain why they are not feasible.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete for a paper emphasizing hardware-aware scalability. The latency analysis is mainly branch-level; end-to-end throughput, prefill latency, memory usage, and quality-efficiency Pareto curves versus dense FlashAttention and other sparse baselines are not sufficiently reported.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, especially claims of significant advancement and near-linear scalability. The compression branch is identified as the main bottleneck, and several attention-scaling configurations collapse to 0.0 without enough diagnosis.

Reproducibility is weaker than desired: the abstract leaves project/code/model links blank, training requires 4600 H100 GPU hours, dataset filtering details are limited, and several implementation/kernel details needed to reproduce the hardware-aware results are underspecified.

The paper has presentation issues, including typos, formatting problems in tables, duplicated or mismatched table captions, and occasional unclear notation. These do not invalidate the work but reduce confidence in polish and reproducibility.

Main performance gains are often modest. On LongVideoBench and MLVU the improvements over strong sparse baselines are small, and VideoNSA is not consistently better than all reported external models despite broad claims of advancing or outperforming existing methods.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: scaling video-language models to long video contexts without discarding potentially important visual tokens.

The proposed hybrid design is technically plausible: applying learnable Native Sparse Attention to visual tokens while preserving dense/GQA behavior for text is a reasonable engineering choice for video MLLMs.

The empirical section covers several relevant benchmark families, including long-video understanding, temporal reasoning, spatial reasoning, scaling studies, branch ablations, gate analyses, and latency/FLOP measurements.

Some results are positive, especially on LongTimeScope, Tomato, and VSIBench relative to the dense Qwen2.5-VL baseline, suggesting that learned sparse routing can help certain long-context video tasks.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. The main contribution appears to be an adaptation of an existing Native Sparse Attention mechanism to Qwen2.5-VL video tokens, with relatively little new modeling insight beyond modality-specific application and engineering.

The central empirical comparison is confounded: VideoNSA is end-to-end trained on 216K video QA pairs, while many token-compression and sparse-attention baselines are training-free. The dense SFT baseline performs worse than the original model, which makes it hard to separate benefits of the sparse architecture from training recipe, data quality, and implementation choices.

Performance gains are often modest. On the main table, VideoNSA is only slightly better than Qwen2.5-VL or prior sparse baselines on several benchmarks, is not best on all metrics, and the claimed broad superiority is stronger than the evidence supports.

Efficiency claims are not fully convincing. The paper emphasizes sparse attention and theoretical FLOP reductions, but actual latency is affected by kernel padding and implementation overhead; VideoNSA is not clearly dominant over all sparse alternatives in practical inference efficiency.

Reproducibility is weak for a paper requiring 4600 H100 GPU hours. The project page, code, and model fields are blank, no released artifacts are evident, and there is no clear reporting of seeds, variance, or statistical significance.

The evaluation lacks enough controlled comparisons: there is no strong trained sparse baseline under the same data and compute budget, no comparison to training dense attention with a better-matched recipe, and limited analysis of whether improvements come from NSA, longer context allocation, or fine-tuning effects.

Several claims are overextended, such as 'reliable scaling to 128K' and attention-sink interpretations, without enough rigorous causal evidence. Some analyses are interesting but feel descriptive rather than decisive.

Presentation quality is below top-tier expectations: there are many typos, spacing/formatting issues, awkward phrasing, duplicated or mislabeled-looking tables in the appendix, and incomplete front-matter links, all of which reduce confidence in the care of the submission.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck in video-language models: scaling long video context without destructive token dropping. Adapting Native Sparse Attention to video tokens while preserving dense/GQA behavior for text is a sensible and practically motivated design.

The evaluation is broad, covering long video understanding, temporal reasoning, and spatial/spatio-temporal benchmarks, with comparisons to dense Qwen2.5-VL, token compression methods, training-free sparse attention methods, and a same-data dense SFT baseline.

The ablation and analysis sections are unusually extensive. Branch ablations, context allocation studies, attention budget studies, dynamic-vs-static gating, latency breakdowns, and attention sink analyses provide useful evidence that the three-branch learned sparse mechanism is doing meaningful work.

The empirical gains are meaningful on some difficult settings, especially LongTimeScope, Tomato, and VSIBench, where VideoNSA improves over the base Qwen2.5-VL and most sparse/token-compression baselines while using a small fraction of dense attention.
The paper is relevant to both efficient inference and long-context multimodal modeling, and the appendices include many implementation and evaluation details that help interpret the method.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate rather than high: the central technical move is largely an adaptation of NSA to video tokens with modality-specific handling, and the paper would benefit from a sharper account of what is algorithmically new beyond applying/engineering an existing sparse attention mechanism in a video VLM.

Several headline performance gains are modest. On LongVideoBench, MLVU, and TimeScope, improvements over dense Qwen2.5-VL or strong sparse baselines are small, sometimes within a range where variance or evaluation noise could matter, yet statistical uncertainty is not reported.

The comparison set is not fully fair for isolating the value of training. Many baselines are training-free while VideoNSA receives expensive end-to-end training; the dense SFT baseline underperforms, apparently due to data quality, which weakens the conclusion that sparse training itself is the key factor. Stronger trained efficient-video baselines or compute-matched baselines would make the evidence more convincing.

Efficiency claims are promising but somewhat qualified. VideoNSA has large training cost, its practical latency is affected by head padding and kernel inefficiencies, and the reported speedups are not uniformly better than other sparse methods. The paper sometimes overstates near-linear scalability and hardware-awareness relative to the actual implementation results.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a top-tier submission: the title page has blank project/code/model fields, and exact release plans are unclear. Given the engineering-heavy contribution, code, trained weights, and scripts are important for verification.

Some presentation issues reduce confidence: there are many typos/formatting problems, table labeling inconsistencies in the appendix, cramped tables, and occasional overclaims such as “consistently outperforms” despite mixed benchmark/subtask results.

The ethics statement is generic and claims bias/safeguard checks without describing concrete procedures or results. This is not central to the technical contribution, but the claim should be better supported.
